rationale: Judged on the book's own falsifiable method, the case succeeds on both fronts: it dismantles the common reading's scriptural basis and supplies a multi-witness pattern for its own. First, the negative case is strong. The Holy-Spirit identification of lamp oil rests almost entirely on anointing texts (1 Sam 16:13; Acts 10:38; Isa 61:1), yet Exodus 25:6 and 30:22-33 explicitly keep 'oil for the light' and 'anointing oil' as separate provisions with separate compositions and uses — so the anointing-Spirit link does not transfer to the virgins' lamp oil without an unstated step. The strongest common-interpretation proof text, Zechariah 4, never says 'the oil is the Spirit'; the angel's own key identifies the olive branches as 'the two anointed ones,' and the Spirit-word concerns Zerubbabel's work. Meanwhile the parable's mechanics actively resist the Spirit reading: the oil must be bought (Matt 25:9) though the Spirit's gift cannot be purchased (Acts 8:20), must be stored beforehand though the Spirit can fall in a moment (Acts 10:44), and is finite and non-lendable though the Spirit is given 'not by measure' (John 3:34). Second, the positive case meets the recurrence test: Proverbs 21:20 puts oil stored in the dwelling of the wise and spent up by the fool — the parable's exact three terms; Psalm 141:5 calls righteous reproof 'an excellent oil'; Proverbs 27:5-9 moves from rebuke and faithful wounds to ointment and hearty counsel; Proverbs 23:23 commands 'buy the truth... wisdom, and instruction,' matching the parable's otherwise odd 'buy' at Isaiah 55:1-3's price of hearing and obeying; and Proverbs 6:23 supplies lamp = commandment, with Matthew 5:16 supplying light = visible good works. The wise/fool distinction as doer/hearer (Matt 7:24-26) coheres with this. Notably, the book does not deny the Spirit's role but orders it correctly via Ezekiel 36:27 and Galatians 5:22: the Spirit is the cause, the stored obedience is His pressed fruit — which also explains why the oil cannot be borrowed. The common reading, by contrast, is shown to depend on a category confusion between two oils Scripture deliberately separates. No cited counter-text breaks the book's pattern, and the pattern genuinely distinguishes its conclusion from the strongest alternative.
decisive_sources: Exodus 25:6 (lamp oil and anointing oil listed as separate provisions)
Exodus 27:20 with Exodus 30:22-33 (pure beaten oil for light vs. restricted compounded anointing oil)
Matthew 25:3-9 with Acts 8:18-20 and John 3:34 (buy/store/finite/non-transferable mechanics incompatible with the Spirit as referent)
Proverbs 21:20 (oil stored by the wise, spent up by the fool — the parable's three terms)
Proverbs 23:23 with Isaiah 55:1-3 (the command to 'buy' truth, wisdom, and instruction)
Psalm 141:5 and Proverbs 27:5-9 (reproof and counsel figured as oil/ointment)
Proverbs 6:23 and Matthew 5:16 (lamp = commandment; light = visible good works)
Zechariah 4:6-14 (angel identifies the anointed ones, never equates oil with the Spirit)
Ezekiel 36:27 with Galatians 5:22 (Spirit as cause, obedience as His produced fruit)
unresolved_objections: Proverbs 21:20's oil may plausibly be literal wealth/provision in its original sense, weakening it as a symbolic proof text even though the wise/fool/oil triad remains striking.

Zechariah 4's oil flowing through pipes to the lampstand, framed by 'not by might... but by my Spirit,' can still be read as Spirit-supply imagery; the book's handling is plausible but not the only coherent reading.

The academic non-allegorical view — that the 'buy' and the oil are narrative realism for readiness with no fixed referent — is not directly refuted, though the book's method rules it out by premise rather than by argument.

The book's full compound definition ('Spirit-taught truth and correction received, kept, and worked into proven obedience') is richer than what the gathered pattern strictly establishes; the pattern supports 'stored instruction/obedience' more tightly than every clause of the formulation.
